subject: ela
description: Students plan and evaluate the use of multimedia components (graphics, images, charts, music, sound effects) and visual displays in a presentation so that those elements clarify information rather than distract from it. They decide which type of media best supports a given point, judge whether a chosen element actually adds clarity, and explain how a visual or audio element strengthens a spoken message for an audience.
subSkills: Identify the multimedia categories named in the standard (graphics, images, music, sound) and visual displays such as charts, maps, diagrams, and slides
Match a specific multimedia element to the information it is meant to clarify
Judge whether a multimedia or visual element clarifies, supports, or instead distracts from the spoken content
Explain how a chosen element strengthens audience understanding of a particular point
Recommend an improvement when a presentation element is missing, mismatched, or overloaded

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the best media for a point
problemArchetypes.example: A short description of a presentation moment is given (a student explaining how city population changed over ten years). The item asks which multimedia element would most clearly support that point, with options like a line graph, background music, a single photo, and a sound effect.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge clarify vs. distract
problemArchetypes.example: A short scenario describes a slide crowded with flashing animations behind dense text. The item asks whether the element clarifies the information and to identify the reason it helps or hurts.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain the purpose of an element
problemArchetypes.example: A brief passage states that a presenter played a recorded animal call during a talk on bird species. The item asks how that sound clarifies the information for the audience.

problemArchetypes.name: Diagnose and fix a weak choice
problemArchetypes.example: A scenario describes a presenter reading aloud a long list of numbers with no visual. The item asks which visual display would best clarify the data and why.

problemArchetypes.name: Match element to category
problemArchetypes.example: A short list of presentation elements is given. The item asks the student to sort or label which are visual displays and which are audio components, or to name the category an element belongs to.

stimulusRules.selfContained: Every item must embed the full scenario, presentation description, or short passage it depends on directly in the item text. The student needs nothing external: no live presentation, no video, no separate slide deck. Any 'multimedia element' is described in words within the item.

passageLengthByDifficulty.easy: 1 to 2 sentences describing a single presentation moment or a short labeled list of elements.
passageLengthByDifficulty.medium: 3 to 5 sentences describing a presentation scenario with one element to evaluate and some surrounding context.
passageLengthByDifficulty.hard: 5 to 8 sentences describing a fuller presentation scenario, sometimes with two competing element choices or a sequence of moments to compare and evaluate.

stimulusRules.noMath: Data scenarios may mention numbers (e.g., population figures) only as context for choosing a visual; students are never asked to compute. No calculation is required.

Easy.description: Identify-level tasks from a 1 to 2 sentence stimulus. Student recognizes a media category or picks the obviously appropriate element when the answer is direct and the distractors are clearly mismatched.
constraints: Stimulus is 1 to 2 sentences or a short labeled list
Task verb is identify, name, or match
Only one element plausibly fits; wrong options are obviously off-topic or the wrong sense (audio vs. visual)
No inference about audience effect required

Medium.description: Analyze-level tasks from a 3 to 5 sentence scenario. Student selects the best media for a specific point or explains how a given element clarifies information, requiring some inference about how the element connects to the content.
constraints: Stimulus is 3 to 5 sentences with surrounding context
Task verb is analyze, explain, or determine which best clarifies
Two options are partially plausible, requiring the student to reason about fit
Student must connect the element to the specific information it clarifies

Hard.description: Evaluate-level tasks from a 5 to 8 sentence scenario. Student judges whether an element clarifies or distracts, compares two competing choices, or diagnoses a weak presentation and recommends the improvement that best serves the audience.
constraints: Stimulus is 5 to 8 sentences, possibly with two competing elements or a sequence
Task verb is evaluate, compare, justify, or revise
Distractors reflect plausible but flawed reasoning, not obvious errors
Student must weigh clarity against distraction and justify the judgment

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes any added media automatically improves a presentation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that selects an element simply because it adds visual or audio interest, ignoring whether it clarifies the actual point (e.g., picks lively background music for a data explanation because it makes the talk more exciting)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses decorative or entertaining media with media that clarifies information
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that values an element for being attractive or fun rather than for making the information easier to understand (e.g., picks a colorful unrelated image over a clear chart)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student mismatches the media type to the kind of information
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that pairs the wrong category with the content, such as choosing a sound effect to show how a quantity changed over time, or a photo to display detailed numerical comparisons

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes more elements are always better and ignores clutter or distraction
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that rates a crowded, overloaded slide as effective because it contains many elements, missing that the clutter hides the main idea

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks visuals are only for decoration and never essential to meaning
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that treats a clarifying chart or diagram as optional or merely decorative, concluding the spoken words alone are enough even when the data is hard to follow by ear
